claims.text: The material is a tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy intended for fusion plasma-facing components.
The initial alloy is a homogeneous, supersaturated solid solution without pre-engineered coherent nanoprecipitates.
Stepwise controlled processing can induce coherent nanoprecipitation in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys.
Temperatures near or above 800 °C are relevant conditions for evaluating these plasma-facing alloys.
The treatment produces precipitates with clean, semi-coherent interfaces distributed throughout grains and along grain boundaries.
Coherent precipitate interfaces facilitate dislocation transmission.
Coherent precipitate interfaces relieve stress concentrations.
The coherent interfaces promote mild work hardening.
Relieving interfacial stress concentrations delays premature crack initiation.
The nanoprecipitate-mediated mechanism delays crack propagation.
The nanoprecipitate interfaces govern both plastic strain tolerance and toughness at high temperature.
Relative to an untreated or conventionally processed control, the precipitate-treated alloy will have higher yield strength at high temperature.
Relative to the control, the precipitate-treated alloy will have improved plastic strain tolerance at high temperature.
Relative to the control, the precipitate-treated alloy will have enhanced fracture toughness at high temperature.
The mechanism should hold around 800 °C and above when diffusion is active and coherent precipitates stabilize the microstructure.
The mechanism cannot confidently be extrapolated to other alloy families or extreme irradiation conditions.
The optimal nanoprecipitate size, distribution, and interface characteristics have not been determined.
Irradiation and oxidation may alter the proposed high-temperature mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and mechanism identify coherent interfaces, whereas the structural mediator describes the interfaces as semi-coherent; the intended interface coherency is therefore internally inconsistent.
